html:
From about 1912 Ibn Saud settled nomadic Bedouin of central Arabia in farming colonies called hijras. The settlers were called the Ikhwan, "the Brethren".

Preachers taught them the strict teachings of Wahhabism. In return for land, seed, tools and money, tribesmen gave up camel herding and raiding, built mud houses near wells and mosques, and tried farming. The first hijra was at al-Artawiya in the Nejd; dozens more followed.

The colonies gave Ibn Saud a loyal and zealous army that could gather quickly. Ikhwan fighters won his wars against rival Arabian rulers and took the Hejaz in 1924 to 1925. But they also raided into British-ruled Iraq and Transjordan and opposed new things like cars and the telegraph. When they rebelled, Ibn Saud crushed them at the battle of Sabilla in 1929.

The hijras are an early example of the push to settle herders that changed the nomadic life of Arabia within a few generations.
sum: From about 1912 Ibn Saud settled nomadic Bedouin of central Arabia in farming colonies called hijras. The settlers were called the Ikhwan, "the Brethren".
